source_text: Τὸ δ᾿ αἴτιον τῆς Ἰουδαίων περιτομῆς οὐ ταὐτὸν ἐστι τῷ αἰτίῳ τῆς Αἰγυπτίων περιτομῆς ἢ Κόλχων· διὸ οὐχ ἡ αὐτὴ νομισθείη ἂν περιτομή. καὶ ὥσπερ ὁ θύων οὐ τῷ αὐτῷ θύει, εἰ καὶ ὁμοίως θύειν δοκεῖ. καὶ ὁ εὐχόμενος οὐ τῷ αὐτῷ εὔχεται, εἰ καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ἐν ταῖς εὐχαῖς ἀξιοῖ· οὕτως οὐδ᾿ εἴ τις περιτέμνεται, ἀδιαφορεῖ πάντως τῆς πρὸς ἕτερον περιτομῆς. ἡ γὰρ πρόθεσις καὶ ὁ νόμος καὶ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ περιτέμνοντος ἀλλοῖον ποιεῖ τὸ πρᾶγμα. ἵνα δ᾿ ἔτι μᾶλλον νοηθῇ τὸ κατὰ τὸν τόπον, λεκτέον ὅτι τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὄνομα ταὐτὸν μέν ἐστι παρὰ πᾶσιν Ἕλλησιν· ἤδη δὲ ἀποδείκνυται ἄλλη μὲν ἡ κατ᾿ Ἐπίκουρον δικαιοσύνη, ἄλλη δὲ ἡ κατὰ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς, ἀρνουμένους τὸ τριμερὲς τῆς ψυχῆς, ἄλλη δὲ κατὰ τοὺς ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος, ἰδιοπραγίαν τῶν μερῶν τῆς ψυχῆς φάσκοντας εἶναι τὴν δικαιοσύνην. οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἄλλη μὲν ἡ Ἐπικούρου ἀνδρεία, ὑπομένοντος πόνους διὰ φυγὴν πόνων πλειόνων, ἄλλη δ᾿ ἡ τοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς, δι᾿ αὐτὴν αἱρουμένου πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν. ἄλλη δ᾿ ἡ ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος, τοῦ θυμικοῦ μέρους τῆς ψυχῆς φάσκοντος αὐτὴν εἶναι ἀρετὴν καὶ ἀποτάσσοντος αὐτῇ τόπον τὸν περὶ τὸν θώρακα. οὕτως δ᾿ εἴη ἂν κατὰ τὰ διάφορα τῶν περιτεμνομένων δόγματα διάφορος ἡ περιτομὴ, περὶ ἧς ἐν τοιούτῳ συγγράμματι οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον νῦν λέγειν· ὅτῳ γὰρ φίλον ἰδεῖν τὰ κινήσαντα ἡμᾶς εἰς τὸν τόπον, ἀναγνώτω περὶ αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς εἰς τὴν πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐπιστολὴν Παύλου πραγματευθεῖσιν ἡμῖν.
thought_title: The same rite can have different meanings
pass_a_gloss: The cause (αἴτιον) of the circumcision (περιτομῆς) of Jews is not the same as the cause of the circumcision of Egyptians or Colchians; therefore it would not be thought (νομισθείη) the same circumcision. And as the one sacrificing (θύων) does not sacrifice to the same, even if he seems to sacrifice similarly, and the one praying does not pray to the same, even if he asks (ἀξιοῖ) the same things in the prayers, thus not even if someone is circumcised does it altogether not differ (ἀδιαφορεῖ πάντως) from the circumcision toward another (πρὸς ἕτερον). For the purpose (πρόθεσις) and the law (νόμος) and the intention (βούλημα) of the one circumcising makes the thing (πρᾶγμα) other (ἀλλοῖον). That what concerns the passage (τόπον) may be understood still more, it must be said that the name of justice (δικαιοσύνης) is the same among all Greeks; but it is shown that justice according to Epicurus is other, other that according to those from the Stoa, denying the tripartite (τριμερές) of the soul (ψυχῆς), other according to those from Plato, saying justice to be the doing of its own (ἰδιοπραγίαν) by the parts of the soul. Thus also other the courage (ἀνδρεία) of Epicurus, enduring pains (πόνους) through flight (φυγήν) of more pains, other that of the one from the Stoa, choosing all virtue (ἀρετήν) for its own sake, other that from Plato, saying it to be virtue of the spirited (θυμικοῦ) part of the soul and assigning (ἀποτάσσοντος) it the place about the chest (θώρακα). Thus would circumcision be different according to the different doctrines (δόγματα) of those circumcised, about which in such a treatise (συγγράμματι) it is not necessary now to speak; for whoever wishes to see the things that moved (κινήσαντα) us to the subject, let him read about it in things worked out (πραγματευθεῖσιν) by us on the epistle of Paul to the Romans.

choices.english: not in every case the same
choices.why: οὐδ᾿ ... ἀδιαφορεῖ πάντως: 'by no means the same' (too absolute) -> 'not in every case the same'; 'with reference to another' -> 'directed to another'

pass_b_english: The reason for the circumcision of the Jews is not the same as the reason for the circumcision of the Egyptians or of the Colchians, and so it could not be thought the same circumcision. Just as one who sacrifices does not sacrifice to the same being, even if he seems to sacrifice in the same way, and one who prays does not pray to the same being, even if he asks for the same things in his prayers, so too, when someone is circumcised, it is not in every case the same as circumcision directed to another. For the purpose, the law and the intention of the one who circumcises make the act different.

To make the point of this subject still clearer, it must be said that the name of justice is the same among all the Greeks; yet it is shown that justice according to Epicurus is one thing; justice according to the Stoics, who deny that the soul has three parts, is another; and justice according to the Platonists, who say that justice is each part of the soul doing its own work, is another again. So too the courage of Epicurus, who endures pains to escape greater pains, is one thing; the courage of the Stoic, who chooses every virtue for its own sake, is another; and courage according to Plato, who says that it is the virtue of the spirited part of the soul and assigns to it a place about the chest, is another again.

In the same way circumcision would differ according to the different doctrines of those who are circumcised. About this it is not necessary to speak now in a work of this kind; whoever wishes to see what moved us on this subject may read what we have written about it in our treatment of Paul's Epistle to the Romans.
notes: Answers Celsus's claim (5.41) that circumcision came from the Egyptians and Colchians. 'Directed to another' renders τῆς πρὸς ἕτερον περιτομῆς, parallel to sacrificing and praying 'to the same' being; οὐδ᾿ ... ἀδιαφορεῖ πάντως ('nor is it in every case no different') is rendered 'not in every case the same', since the argument is that intention, not the act, decides the difference. τὸν τόπον here means the subject under discussion, not a passage. Philosophical references, not quotations, so no inline source given: Platonic justice as each part doing its own work (ἰδιοπραγία), compare Plato, Republic 4.433a-b and 441d-e; spirit lodged in the chest, compare Timaeus 70a. 'Those from Plato' and 'the Stoics' are schools, while for courage the Greek names Plato himself (φάσκοντος agrees with Πλάτωνος). The Romans work is Origen's Commentary on Romans (on Romans 2:25-29); no Scripture verse is quoted here.

changes: οὐδ᾿ ... ἀδιαφορεῖ πάντως: 'by no means the same' (too absolute) -> 'not in every case the same'; 'with reference to another' -> 'directed to another'
'the courage of Plato' -> 'courage according to Plato' (doctrine, not Plato's personal courage)
